extracted.intended_audience: romance authors, aspiring writers, RWA members, and general readers researching the Romance Writers of America
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize RWA's definitions, membership and award/contest rules relevant to producing and evaluating romance novels (what counts as a romance, membership tracks, award submission/judging practices, and related fairness/diversity criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Romance novel core definition (RWA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main plot of a romance novel must revolve around the two people as they develop romantic love for each other and work to build a relationship together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the conflict and the climax of the novel should be directly related to that core theme of developing a romantic relationship, although the novel can also contain subplots that do not specifically relate to the main characters' romantic love. (Original wording: 'the main plot of a romance novel must revolve around the two people as they develop romantic love for each other and work to build a relationship together.' )

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotionally satisfying and optimistic ending (happy ending requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A romance novel must have an 'emotionally satisfying and optimistic ending.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RWA (and many publishers) embrace a definition that includes focus on a developing romantic relationship plus an optimistic ending; debate exists about when exceptions (e.g., Romeo and Juliet) are acceptable, but the organization's standard requires a happy/optimistic resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict and climax tied to the romantic relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the conflict and the climax of the novel should be directly related to the core theme of developing the romantic relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While subplots are allowed, the central dramatic tension and the story's turning point must be about the main couple's relationship (i.e., what is at stake and what is resolved should be their relationship).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commonly cited additional genre conventions (controversial/traditional constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors/readers believe additional restrictions apply to romance novels, such as protagonists meeting early in the story, avoiding themes like adultery, and favoring heterosexual pairings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are debated conventions rather than universal rules; the general RWA/publisher definition focuses on the relationship + optimistic ending, but many widely considered romances deviate from stricter constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: RWA membership eligibility (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are eligible to join the RWA if they are actively pursuing a career writing romance novels; both published authors and those with complete but unpublished manuscripts may be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry professionals and aspiring authors who have not completed a manuscript can join as non-voting associate members; booksellers and librarians can join as non-voting affiliate members. All members receive the RWA magazine.

rubrics_metrics.name: RWA membership tracks: PRO vs PAN requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are divided into two membership tracks: PRO for authors who have completed a manuscript but not yet published it; PAN (Published Author Network) for authors who have published and met a set earnings threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PAN members must have seen their novels published in print and have earned a set threshold from royalties or advances. Authors who use vanity publishers that offer little or no editing/promotional help do not qualify for PAN.

rubrics_metrics.name: Golden Heart contest structure and judging (unpublished authors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Golden Heart contest honors unpublished authors; the first round is judged by a panel of RWA members, and one hundred manuscripts are chosen as finalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The finalists' manuscripts are then judged by acquiring editors from romance publishing houses. Historically, about 30% of Golden Heart finalists find their work accepted by print publishers. The award recognizes excellence among unpublished manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: RITA (and Vivian) Awards: submission and category structure (published works)
rubrics_metrics.description: The RITA Award (replaced in 2021 by the Vivian Award) recognized excellence in multiple categories of romantic fiction; authors and editors submit published works for consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works are entered into one of many specific categories (e.g., Long Contemporary Romance, Romantic Suspense). Finalists are announced and winners are presented with a statuette. Authors who have won at least three RITA Awards within a specific category are inducted into the RWA Hall of Fame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall of Fame induction criterion for awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who have won at least three RITA Awards within a specific category are inducted into the RWA Hall of Fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a categorical track-based lifetime recognition (examples: Nora Roberts, Jo Beverley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Award entry/judging conflicts and procedural shortcomings
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrants could pay to nominate books and entrants could elect to judge other nominees, creating potential conflicts of interest and integrity issues in contest judging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically judges were not provided with training on scoring or avoiding bias, and these procedural weaknesses contributed to controversies over representativeness and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contest judging fairness reforms and recommended judge composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Reforms introduced to address bias included tracking scores by individual judges to detect bias and requiring that some judges in each category be librarians or booksellers and that at least one judge be a person of color or a queer person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures are described as attempts to make judging more representative and to reduce systemic bias in award outcomes; they follow analysis showing extremely low representation of Black authors among finalists and winners.
